extracted.intended_audience: painters, architects, art students, and patrons advocating artistic (especially Gothic) revival
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on how painters and architects should finish works, use color, and judge artistic value, with specific advocacy for a Gothic/Christian architectural revival and practical cautions about where to begin. Emphases include how finish should engage the imagination, the primacy of rightly-used color, motives for making art, and concrete prescriptions for architectural practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish should be suggestive and add ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: "Observe, then, whenever finish is given for the sake of realization, it is wrong; whenever it is given for the sake of adding ideas it is right. All true finish consists in the addition of ideas, that is to say, in giving the imagination more food."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finish ought to summon and feed the viewer's imagination rather than merely substituting the artist's labor for the imaginative act. Finishing that merely substantiates an idea insults the imagination and is therefore wrong; true finish multiplies subjects of thought and provides 'more food' for imagination. (See also admonition that what is done merely 'to realize and substantiate an idea is impertinent'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage the imagination with selective, guiding details
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist should neither leave the imagination to itself nor insult it by full realization; instead he should give a few vigorous touches and then provide select completed details that the imagination cannot easily supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical method (oak example): supply a few strokes/dashes to suggest a tree, draw a cluster or two of leaves or a couple of acorns perfectly, gild a few near edges for sunshine, and indicate a single prominent bird — then let the viewer's imagination fill the rest. This balances guidance and freedom: give enough help where imagination lacks, but leave the greater part to the viewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid finish for mere realization or deceptive exactness
rubrics_metrics.description: Realization pursued for its own sake (detailed, deceptive realism intended to make the work appear like the thing itself) is vulgar and wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hobbima's laborious foliage and bark that attempt to 'deceive' the eye are condemned; black outlines on white forcing the imagination should not be undermined by needless factual completion. The artist who attempts to make a work 'more real' than necessary takes 'the food out of [the imagination's] mouth.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour must be right, dominant, and only used by those who understand it
rubrics_metrics.description: "Wherever [colour] enters it must take the mastery, and, whatever else is sacrificed for its sake, it, at least, must be right... If that be wrong, all is wrong."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colour is a supreme power in art: if used it must be lovely and true, because right colour can redeem weakness, while false colour ruins the whole work. Only touch colour if you can command it (be 'a master, up to a certain point'). Better an inferior sketch than a badly coloured painting. More realization can be allowed when done for colour's sake, but never add colour merely to increase realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not add colour merely to increase realization
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawing or engraving is often all that the imagination needs; to 'paint' merely to make a subject more real is to insult the imaginative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colour should be introduced for its own expressive and aesthetic power, not as a tool to make things look more factual. If the artist has not loved or understood colour but uses it only to 'complete' the picture, he commits a double sin: dulling imagination and oppressing it with false colour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate art chiefly as expression of one soul to another
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whatever may be the means, or whatever the more immediate end of any kind of art, all of it that is good agrees in this, that it is the expression of one soul talking to another, and is precious according to the greatness of the soul that utters it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should be judged by the spirit and intent behind it rather than narrowly by manual skill, faithful imitation, or adherence to technical rules. This broader test enables reverence across periods and styles and frees the critic from limiting admiration to a few technical masters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid practicing or valuing art chiefly for human praise or vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists should not make knowledge, passion, or art subservient to the desire of praise; sacrificing true pleasure (especially pleasure in colour and form) for fame is harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that modern civilisation tempts artists to abandon simple, true delights for vanity. The proper motive for art is love of its true delights and, for moral persons, 'God's and the conscience's' praise rather than man's applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture must serve daily life and address all minds
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture uniquely answers practical daily needs and can 'address every character of mind in the spectator,' being the property of all and forcing itself into notice even in languid moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike pictures or statues (which can be private), the outsides of houses belong to the passer-by; therefore architecture should be substantial, benevolent in public effect, and designed to engage a wide public, not just narrow aesthetic tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject Greek, Roman, and Renaissance (classical) architectural principles for revival
rubrics_metrics.description: "First, let us cast out utterly whatever is connected with the Greek, Roman, or Renaissance architecture, in principle or in form... Whatever has any connexion with the five orders...whatever betrays the smallest respect for Vitruvian laws, or conformity with Palladian work — that we are to endure no more."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin prescribes a wholesale rejection of classical orders and Greco-Roman models, arguing they are lifeless, pagan in origin, and unchristian in revival. This is the first step toward re-establishing a living, moral architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt Gothic ('Christian') architecture for civil and domestic buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic architecture is described as animated, serviceable, honorable, flexible to duty, enduring, instructive, and capable of addressing all emotions and workmen: 'In this architecture let us henceforward build, alike the church, the palace, and the cottage; but chiefly let us use it for our civil and domestic buildings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin urges building principally in English/French thirteenth-century Gothic forms, applied especially to civil and domestic projects to win public acceptance. He counsels humility, accepting help from simple workmen, combining northern Gothic forms with Italian refinement, and seeking floral and inlaid ornament executed with modern wealth and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use churches as primary sites for experimental Gothic revival
rubrics_metrics.description: Temples/churches are not the proper scenes for experiments in untried architecture; their use as testing grounds arouses prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce Gothic chiefly through civil/domestic architecture to avoid provoking religious or partisan resistance. Churches should be preserved from experimental failures; successful civil examples will help persuade wider acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postpone architectural figure-sculpture; emphasize floral and inlaid work
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern dress and lack of suitable living models make architectural figure-sculpture presently impracticable ('we have no figures to study from'), but 'in floral sculpture we may go far beyond what has yet been done.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus early revival efforts on elements that can be executed well now (floral carving, inlaid work, refined execution of details) rather than on figure-sculpture which requires appropriate costume and study from living models; use modern wealth and science to achieve high craftsmanship.
